pr_title: Revert "Ensure there is one running static pod with the same full name"
pr_body:
Reverts kubernetes/kubernetes#104743 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/107695

Issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/107733

```release-note
Reverts handling of static pod fullnames that may sometimes cause static pods to fail to restart.
```
pr_comments:
/kind regression
/priority critical-urgent

@ehashman: /release-note-edit must be used with a single release note block.

<details>

In response to [this](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/107734#issuecomment-1020489430):

>I think the revert makes sense.
>
>I noticed when I was trying to add coverage for https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/107695 that we added `newStaticPod` here in the test coverage but not `newStaticPodWithPhase` to match the existing mocks: 
>
>
>We lack coverage for this: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5426da8f69c1d5fa99814526c1878aeb99b2456e/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L572-L576
>
>So @rphillips tried to add in the missing pod fullname, but I'm not 100% sure we have a reproducer that can catch that.
>
>I started adding a case:
>
>```diff
>diff --git a/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers_test.go b/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers_test.go
>index 4028c06c292..fc5f975acfd 100644
>--- a/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers_test.go
>+++ b/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers_test.go
>@@ -164,6 +164,21 @@ func newStaticPod(uid, name string) *v1.Pod {
>        }
> }
> 
>+func newStaticPodWithPhase(uid, name string, phase v1.PodPhase) *v1.Pod {
>+       return &v1.Pod{
>+               ObjectMeta: metav1.ObjectMeta{
>+                       UID:  types.UID(uid),
>+                       Name: name,
>+                       Annotations: map[string]string{
>+                               kubetypes.ConfigSourceAnnotationKey: kubetypes.FileSource,
>+                       },
>+               },
>+               Status: v1.PodStatus{
>+                       Phase: phase,
>+               },
>+       }
>+}
>+
> // syncPodRecord is a record of a sync pod call
> type syncPodRecord struct {
>        name       string
>@@ -856,6 +871,24 @@ func Test_allowPodStart(t *testing.T) {
>                        },
>                        allowed: true,
>                },
>+               {
>+                       desc: "static pod if the static pod is terminated and rebooting",
>+                       pod:  newStaticPodWithPhase("uid-0", "foo", v1.PodSucceeded),
>+                       podSyncStatuses: map[types.UID]*podSyncStatus{
>+                               "uid-0": {
>+                                       fullname: "foo_",
>+                               },
>+                       },
>+                       // waitingToStartStaticPodsByFullname: map[string][]types.UID{
>+                       //      "foo_": {
>+                       //              types.UID("uid-0"),
>+                       //      },
>+                       // },
>+                       startedStaticPodsByFullname: map[string]types.UID{
>+                               "foo_": types.UID("uid-0"),
>+                       },
>+                       allowed: true,
>+               },
>        }
> 
>        for _, tc := range testCases {
>```
>
>But then I realized that we don't have anything mocking the worker [podCache](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5426da8f69c1d5fa99814526c1878aeb99b2456e/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L575), which will be necessary to give proper coverage, and so we probably have a whole matrix of missing test cases. Hence, I think it might be easiest to revert for now.
>
>/lgtm
>/cc @gjkim42 
>/triage accepted
>
>/release-note-edit
>```release-note
>Reverts handling of static pod fullnames that may sometimes cause static pods to fail to restart.
>```

/hold

The original commit was also backported to 1.22 (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/106394). Will this revert also be backported? Does this reintroduce any regressions to the 1.22 and 1.23 streams?

> The original commit was also backported to 1.22 (#106394). Will this revert also be backported? Does this reintroduce any regressions to the 1.22 and 1.23 streams?

If we revert, I think the reverts should be backported.

The patch was intended to fix https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/97722#issuecomment-888717438 which sounds like the current failure mode we're seeing in OpenShift, so that fix did not work in all cases. We discovered that we are still seeing some affected workloads in https://prow.ci.openshift.org/view/gs/origin-ci-test/pr-logs/pull/26796/pull-ci-openshift-origin-master-e2e-aws-serial/1487126569716551680

Taking https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/107695 was low risk and did help, but per my concerns in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/107734#issuecomment-1020489430 I think that we missed an entire matrix of test coverage because code that was not changed was affected by this change and missed in review.

Given all of this, our options are:
- revert
- try to figure out a fix forward

The problem is, I'm not sure what a quick forward fix would be :)

First I can't dig this issue as there is no clear reproducer.

> https://prow.ci.openshift.org/view/gs/origin-ci-test/pr-logs/pull/26796/pull-ci-openshift-origin-master-e2e-aws-serial/1487126569716551680

I am not sure what this CI job was doing, but I guess the CI job was trying to restart an etcd pod which is a static pod. Am I right?
Does the job always fail? or sometimes?


> Given all of this, our options are:
> 
> * revert
> * try to figure out a fix forward
> 
> The problem is, I'm not sure what a quick forward fix would be :)

**_I think at least we have to confirm that this PR(reverting) can address the problem._**

Found a reproducer here. 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/107733#issuecomment-1024895999
e2e test: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/107855

And made a fix for it.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/107854

Maybe the fix could be an alternative.

> First I can't dig this issue as there is no clear reproducer.
> 
> I am not sure what this CI job was doing, but I guess the CI job was trying to restart an etcd pod which is a static pod. Am I right? Does the job always fail? or sometimes?

I believe the reproducer is to delete and recreate the static pod multiple times, such that we hit a race between teardown and setup. We are seeing that sometimes the new static pod never comes up, such as in the linked run above.

@rphillips has confirmed through some local testing that a revert fixes the issue we're seeing, whereas other patches still seem to run into it (e.g. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/107854#issuecomment-1025950222)

Are we sure that this patch fixes the bug in question? We had a lot of other patches go in from Clayton in this release, it's possible that this bug this intended to fix was already fixed elsewhere. 

I think right now the best path forward is to revert this, add test coverage that demonstrates the problem, and then add a patch that fixes the problem. The original PR here only added unit tests and did not add an e2e loop with static pods.

/lgtm

/hold cancel

+1 with @ehashman ... We need to revisit the original PR and get more testing around it.

So one serious concern here is that the fix was addressing a demonstrable hard break in static pods.  If we've regressed elsewhere, reverting just moves the problem around (doesn't result in fewer problems).  I'd prefer to spend a small amount of time and find a fix, while at the same time improving the test coverage based on our new failure mode.

> So one serious concern here is that the fix was addressing a demonstrable hard break in static pods. If we've regressed elsewhere, reverting just moves the problem around (doesn't result in fewer problems). I'd prefer to spend a small amount of time and find a fix, while at the same time improving the test coverage based on our new failure mode.

I believe the demonstrable break was your PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/104847 which fixed https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/104648. I think there may be some mixed communication around bugs and patches which caused this patch to land; it is not clear to me what this is actually fixing, and it's definitely causing a regression.

/test pull-kubernetes-e2e-gce-ubuntu-containerd
+1 the original PR clearly regresses the static pods, and the reasoning behind the issue may have been fixed in the followup pod lifecycle PRs we fixed last year.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/104743#issuecomment-915332807 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/104743#issuecomment-916175110 summarizes why that fix is necessary - we don't want people to use static UIDs with static pods, and we want the "obvious correct behavior".  All static pod updates look like force deletion on the apiserver to the kubelet - the old version disappears, the new version is held on the kubelet until the old version completes.  Therefore, reverting #104743 would allow static pods without static uids to be reentrant, which is surprising.

The attached fix looks correct, and after reviewing the test it also seems to reproduce the problem described.  I had some additional feedback on the issue, but I don't think a revert is appropriate until we determine the fix has further issues or there is another issue buried underneath it.

@smarterclayton Prior to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/104743 there is logic to prevent static pods of the same [name to be started](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blame/1e4cacb57743514ffbc45dcdb1abe5797b4d1a97/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L381). The name is derived from the [namespace]_[pod name] tuple. This check would prevent the static uid from being re-entrant since the block is just derived from the tuple and not the UID.

> @smarterclayton Prior to #104743 there is logic to prevent static pods of the same [name to be started](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blame/1e4cacb57743514ffbc45dcdb1abe5797b4d1a97/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L381). The name is derived from the [namespace]_[pod name] tuple. This check would prevent the static uid from being re-entrant since the block is just derived from the tuple and not the UID.

I guess that the logic has not been enough to prevent the new static pod to be reentrant, and #104743 was intended to guarantee the graceful termination of a static pod.

I can understand that this bug is more urgent to be fixed. However, the graceful termination of a static pod that #104743 wanted to guarantee should be fixed someday unless we decide not to support it.

@gjkim42 I'm confused as to the ordering of events. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/97722 was opened prior to the pod lifecycle refactor, and I think we handled this case. I believe https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/97722 should have been closed. Is there a known test case that failed?
@gjkim42 Didn't this patch fix it? https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/d5719800bf044b67a538c679dbd808def36bcf0f

@rphillips 
No to my knowledge. They are different issues.

One handles the recreation of static pods having the same uid with the same fullname(technically one pod).
The other(#97722) handles the recreation(terminate one and create the other) of static pods having the different uids with the same fullname(technically two pods).

@gjkim42 After reviewing the original PR, I noticed this [change in logic](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/104743/files#diff-c6d21f5481c391a3f32bcfddf45c9c20132b2876e8be9690289474b76b71d809L902-L904). completeTerminating does not cleanup startedStaticPodsByFullname, when it did cleanup terminatingStaticPodFullnames before. I tested a build with [similar cleanup logic](https://github.com/openshift/kubernetes/pull/1157/commits/dbfcc1aefdbf03a366eadf7175444cbbc986fa6a) and it does seem to help the issue.

> @gjkim42 After reviewing the original PR, I noticed this [change in logic](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/104743/files#diff-c6d21f5481c391a3f32bcfddf45c9c20132b2876e8be9690289474b76b71d809L902-L904). completeTerminating does not cleanup startedStaticPodsByFullname, when it did cleanup terminatingStaticPodFullnames before. I tested a build with [similar cleanup logic](https://github.com/openshift/kubernetes/pull/1157/commits/dbfcc1aefdbf03a366eadf7175444cbbc986fa6a) and it does seem to help the issue.

@rphillips 
I think the logic is technically the same as it was. [This logic](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/104743/files#diff-c6d21f5481c391a3f32bcfddf45c9c20132b2876e8be9690289474b76b71d809L501-L516) complements the change.
Removing a static pod from startedStaticPodsByFullname in completeTerminating function is not what we want to do.
closing in favor of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/107900

issue_context.title: 1.22 regression: removing and recreating static pod manifest leaves pod in error state
issue_context.body:
#### What happened:

* Started a 1.22 cluster
* Added a static pod manifest
* Observed the pod run successfully
* Removed and recreated the pod manifest
* Observed the pod enter an error state and never restart successfully

#### What you expected to happen:

For the pod to be re-run successfully (as in previous releases)

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

```
# start a cluster
hack/local-up-cluster.sh

# create a static pod
echo '
kind: Pod
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: mypod
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 1
  containers:
  - name: busybox
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "echo $RANDOM; sleep 100000"]
' > mypod.yaml

sudo cp mypod.yaml /var/run/kubernetes/static-pods/

# wait until the pod is running
watch kubectl get pods -n default

# remove and recreate the static pod
sudo rm /var/run/kubernetes/static-pods/mypod.yaml
sudo cp mypod.yaml /var/run/kubernetes/static-pods/

# observe the pod remain in an error state
watch kubectl get pods -n default
```

#### Anything else we need to know?:

Bisected to 3eadd1a9ead7a009a9abfbd603a5efd0560473cc (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102344)

Broken in 1.22, works in 1.21 and previous versions.

/sig node
cc @smarterclayton @bobbypage @rphillips
comments: I also verified the pending PR fixing the 1.22 [pod admission regression](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/104560) (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/104611) does not fix this issue

The rough structure you described is similar to #104847, except we need to do this for non static pods as well.  There are a couple of problems related to a change like this though because the rest of the Kubelet ONLY references a pod by UID.  So if you were to rapidly delete a pod and create a new one with the same UID AND completely change volumes or devices, it's very likely that other parts of the Kubelet could perform some of their cleanup or tear down logic inconsistently.  I *think* volumes are correct (although that's only if setup and teardown are happening in serial), but I haven't reviewed the others.  Just waiting some unit of time isn't enough - we need to either guarantee those loops are safe for two separate pod definitions with the same UID to be passed to them in quick succession (better testing + review) or we need to add a construct that ensures that those loops don't think the pod is the same (such as a second UID in the kubelet or a generation or something).

The real tension here is that reusing a UID for a completely different instance of a pod (like static pods allow) is not desirable, because UID is supposed to represent an "instance of a pod" and pods provide certain one way guarantees around lifecycle (once a pod is failed, it stays that way forever).  The behavior of static pods shouldn't be modelled like a pod that lives forever, it should be modelled using a controller that stamps out new desired pods (each with their own UID).  However, that's a behavior change, and it's of course possible (but incredibly unlikely) for a duplicate UID to be generated on the apiserver, so the easiest path probably is just "prevent uid reuse from being inconsistent".

In which case, the design of what we're trying to do in Kubelet is:

1. Ensure that the pod worker runs at most one  pod definition with a given uid at a time
2. Ensure that when a pod with a given UID exits, if the pod is still desired with that UID, the new one is started in the pod worker

That's hard to do outside the pod worker today because the loop that drives pod worker is edge driven (change to pod config), not level driven.  We'd need to fix the loop from pod config to pod worker to reconcile the desired state against the actual state, and the kubelet doesn't directly track desired state (because admission decisions aren't recorded in a single list).  But we can't do it from within the pod worker, because we have no idea when the pod worker receives the sequence `STOP(uid=1) -> CREATE(uid=1) -> STOP(uid=1)` whether the second stop cancels the `CREATE` or is simply shortening the first `STOP`.

Probably having pod housekeeping filter the list of desired pods and then have it start any pod that is still desired but is terminated in the Kubelet is the right fix, but I need to think through the tradeoffs some more.  The biggest tradeoff is pod housekeeping happens on a schedule, which means suddenly static pods sharing the same UID that are deleted and recreated suddenly take longer to restart (which I guess is good because it gently penalizes users for using static pod UIDs and doing delete/recreate).

> Note that identical UIDs on static pods pose a problem for calculating pod lifecycle of static pods, tracked in https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1933760#c27
>
> I think the UID reuse here is ultimately the root of the bug, and it breaks assumptions not just here but in the rest of the kubelet.

Elaborating on this a little bit... Right now, we see the following behaviour when a node reboots:

- Static pods terminate, node shuts down
- Node starts up, kubelet does its reconciliation loop
- Static pods are launched prior to API server sync and enter pending state, if the container runtime does not retain information on the previous static pod status [true on OpenShift because we call cri-o wipe, but this could also happen on manual wipe or during disaster recovery]
- New static pods use the same UID as the manifests are unchanged
- Kubelet eventually syncs with API server. Mirror pod with the same UID used to be running, but if it doesn't launch fast enough, kubelet will sync a new Pending status
- Pod illegally transitions back from Running->Pending

So IMO the reuse of the UID is a bit of a hack that breaks core assumptions of the kubelet.

> Pod illegally transitions back from Running->Pending

Turns out this actually is not an illegal transition (which I realized during dealing with soft admission).  A pod that fails soft admission post start is put back into pending because it's not actually running and the kubelet has decided to hold it.  It's strictly better for the kubelet to communicate this because the alternative is a user has no idea that the pod wouldn't be running.  So I think going forward Running -> Pending is a bug when  we're losing state (i.e. restart with wipe) or when we know there is a concrete transition (soft admitted to soft not-admitted)
